Topic.label: Constructing the Perpendicular Bisector of a Segment

Question: Why is the line joining the two intersection points of the arcs the perpendicular bisector? (Construction: Draw arcs centered at $A$ and $B$ with the same radius. The two arcs intersect at $C$ and $D$. Draw $CD$.)

Choices.A: Because $CD$ is parallel and equal in length to $AB$.
Choices.B: Because $C$ and $D$ are two points on segment $AB$.
Choices.C: Each of $C$ and $D$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$. By the criterion, both $C$ and $D$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, and two points determine line $CD$.
Choices.D: Because the radius of the arcs drawn equals the length of $AB$.

Solution:
A point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment lies on its perpendicular bisector. Both $C$ and $D$ satisfy this condition, so line $CD$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

Alternative method 1: Congruent triangles at the midpoint

Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\). Equal compass radii give \(AC=BC\) and \(AD=BD\). Since \(AM=BM\) and \(CM\) is common, \(\triangle ACM\cong\triangle BCM\) by SSS. Their angles at \(M\) are therefore equal. These adjacent angles sum to \(180^\circ\), so each is \(90^\circ\), giving \(CM\perp AB\).

Applying the same argument to \(\triangle ADM\) and \(\triangle BDM\) gives \(DM\perp AB\). The perpendicular through \(M\) is unique, so \(C\), \(M\), and \(D\) lie on that line. Thus \(CD\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\), giving choice C.
